how_to_read: Per-op overrides for the node demo window (nodelab_v2/demo_recipes.py). A node absent here demos itself from its ROLE (codemap/node_roles.json -> demo_recipes.ROLE_DEFAULTS). Keys per op: kind (image|mask|labels|scalar|points|tracks|field|mesh|table|plot|guide), phantom + phantom_kw (nodegraph/phantom.py), prelude (a name from 'preludes' or a list of {op, params, modes}), data_from (tail|src), extra_inputs {socket: {phantom, kw} | {pre: i}}, fixed_params, fixed_modes, sliders {param: [lo, hi]}, live (false -> a Run button), slow_modes {mode: [choices]}, slow_reason, gate_params (selftest only), view {t, z, c}, features (key features / how to use). Validated against the live registry by selftest.test_node_demos.

features: Browse… picks an ND2 or TIFF; the pixel size and Z step are read from the file and shown so you can correct them.
An empty path runs the built-in synthetic stack, so a graph is testable with no file at all.
Grouping = auto grows one output per specimen when the stage log clusters into mosaics.
Access decides whether pixels are read directly or ingested once to a fast on-disk store.
A checkpoint: bake everything upstream to disk once, then re-serve it instead of recomputing.
Live / Held / Docked / Frozen are the four states — the inspector's Dock section switches them.
A docked chain is cut at the dock when the graph runs, so hours of upstream work are never redone.
Writes the Dataset's image (or a named Voxel layer such as a label raster) as a TIFF.
Choose the pyramid level to export a reduced copy; the calibration travels in the file's tags.
Pulling the node is what writes — it is a sink, so it sits at the end of a chain.
Renders a time series (or a Z sweep) to an MP4 / GIF with overlays, a scale bar, a timestamp and channel names.
Up to three sources side by side; the Movie editor in the inspector previews every segment before writing.
Contrast, gamma, fps and the annotation corner are all parameters, so the movie is reproducible from the graph.
Saves a plot node's figure (or any raster) to PNG / PDF / SVG at a chosen dpi.
Wire a plot.* node into it; the frame param picks which timepoint of a time series to save.
A tap that shows whatever is wired into it in the Viewer — up to six sources, switchable.
Scale bar and timestamp overlays are its parameters (size, corner, colour).
Double-click any node, or press F5, to pull it into the Viewer; this node just makes that explicit.
Splits a stream into its parts (image, labels, points, tracks, …) so a page can hand each one on separately.
The part socket names which kind of data comes out; the stream keeps its identity across pages.
Where a page's data comes in: the source menu lists the outputs of the pages before it.
A linked page mirrors its master; edit answers here say whether a change stays local or goes back.
Where a page's results leave: give the output a name and the next page's Input offers it.
Several items can be collected into one output; the optional condition gates when it is published.
The boundary of a collapsed subgraph: what the group receives from the outside.
Select nodes and use Graph → Group (Ctrl+G); Ungroup (Ctrl+Shift+G) opens it again.
The other boundary of a group: what the subgraph hands back out.
A group instance runs the whole subgraph when pulled.
A dot on a wire: pass-through, no computation. Use it to tidy long wires or fan one output out.
Drag from the socket and drop on empty canvas to insert one.
Marks a region of the canvas: nodes inside it are evaluated per frame of the series.
Pair with Repeat In / Repeat Out to loop a sub-chain over t.
The entrance to a repeated zone: everything between this and Repeat Out runs once per iteration.
The zone is unrolled before the engine runs it, so the memo caches each iteration separately.
The exit of a repeated zone: collects every iteration's result back onto one wire.
The entrance to a simulation zone: a sub-chain that is stepped forward, each step fed the last.
Use with Advance to drive the step count.
The exit of a simulation zone: the final state after all steps.
Sweeps up to four sockets of a downstream node over lists, ranges or a percentage around their live defaults.
The metric socket picks the scalar to optimise; the target and tolerance say when to stop.
Each iteration is a separate run in the memo; the var outputs expose the swept values as text.
Steps a simulation zone forward: the probes socket reads a value each step and the node emits it.
Pulls the zone again until the step count is reached.
Stacks several files onto the batch (b) axis so one graph processes all of them identically.
Every node downstream runs per member; Unbatch or Select Batch Member peels them apart again.
Splits a batch back into its members, one output per file.
Picks one member of a batch by index or name.
Chains several files end to end on the time axis — an acquisition saved as one file per hour.
Up to twelve files; the frame interval is carried across the joins.
Keeps the listed channels (here Ch1, the GFP cytoplasm) and drops the rest; the before view shows Ch0.
Pick channels off the Viewer's channel strip with the Pick button.
Grows one output socket per channel so each can feed its own chain.
Wiring an output inserts a Select Channel tap for you at run time.
Joins several datasets along one axis — channels by default, or time, position or Z.
Both inputs here are 1-channel fields; the merged output has two channels.
Datasets that do not line up are refused unless you choose align by index.
Two synthetic fields carry no stage position, so this demo aligns them by index; real files are placed by their stage log.
Keeps the positions of one specimen (a mosaic) from a multipoint file, found by clustering the stage log.
gap_factor decides how far apart two fields must be to count as different specimens.
Keeps one position (M index) of a multipoint file; the index is the position's identity.
Shown: tile B1 (index 2) of a 2×2 stage raster.
Grows one output per position of a multipoint file; wiring one inserts a Select Position tap.
Places every position's tile from the file's stage log (or an explicit grid) and blends the overlaps into one mosaic.
stage+refine phase-correlates each overlapping pair to correct small stage errors.
The output is one position with a larger Y/X extent.
Collapses the series' frames into one stacked volume so a 3-D node can act across time.
Collapses Z into one plane — max, mean, sum, min or median — so a stack can be viewed or segmented flat.
Before: the middle plane of a 7-plane stack. After: the projection.
Keeps a Y/X window (and optionally a Z range and frame list); drag the rectangle on the image with Pick.
The output's axes shrink; every downstream measurement is in the cropped frame.
Crops the data to the stage rectangle another file (the region input) occupies — in absolute microns, so the two files need stage positions.
Shown: a 2×2 stage raster cropped to the field tile B1 covers.
Rescales Y/X (and Z) by a factor; the calibration is restamped so µm stay µm.
Shifts and rotates the image by fixed amounts — the manual counterpart of drift correction.
Measures the global shift of every frame against a reference and shifts it back; the drift is written as a Frame layer.
Before: frame 5 of a drifting series. After: the same frame re-registered to frame 0.
Sub-pixel phase correlation per frame on one reference channel; the per-frame shifts become a Frame layer.
Before: frame 5 of a drifting series. After: stabilized.
Aligns the data to a second dataset (the reference) by phase correlation, within max_shift.
Before: the field shifted by (6, −8) px. After: brought back onto the reference.
Lays every wired file's fields out at their true stage positions on one blank canvas in µm — the primary to chain Overlays onto.
Shown: the canvas spanning a 2×2 stage raster.
Composites a second dataset over the first for comparison: add, over, difference, checkerboard, wipe or flicker.
The offset nudges line the two up; Align by two clicks picks the nudge off the image.
Two synthetic fields carry no stage position, so this demo aligns their centres; real files are placed by stage position, pixel size and focus.
One intensity cut → a 0/1 mask layer named by Output layer; Connected Components turns it into labels.
fixed uses the level you set (eyedropper it off the image); otsu/li/yen/triangle/mean derive it from the histogram.
scope decides which pixels form that histogram: a plane, the volume, the series, the dataset, or each label / ROI.
An adaptive cut: each pixel is compared to the mean of its block, minus an offset — robust to the uneven background.
Splits the histogram into N classes (background, dim, bright…) and keeps the ones you ask for.
Connected components of a mask layer: every touching blob becomes one numbered label.
The two touching nuclei come out as ONE label — that is what Segmentation's watershed fixes.

analysis.segment.slow_reason: StarDist and CellSAM load a neural network; run them with the button
features: One node, four methods: a threshold, a watershed that splits touching objects, StarDist, or CellSAM.
Size floors and ceilings (µm²) drop debris and clumps; fill_holes closes nuclei with dark centres.
Writes a label raster AND a label table (id, area, centroid) under one name.
A threshold expressed on the histogram — percentiles, fractions of full scale, or a window — with clean-up morphology and size limits built in.
The second input (raw) lets you cut on the raw intensities while labelling a processed image.
Press Draw in the node's panel, choose a Tool (rectangle, ellipse, circle, polygon, brush) and an Operation (add / cut), set the brush size, drag on the image, then Apply.
Every shape becomes a numbered region (a label raster plus a table) pinned to the frame it was drawn on; cut carves out of what was drawn before.
Shown: a rectangle with a cut-out, a circle and a polygon, drawn for every frame.
Feed the regions to Measure, to Subtract Background (as a sample of background) or to Crop To.
The same drawing tools as Draw Regions, producing one 0/1 mask instead of numbered regions.
Use it to restrict a threshold (scope = per_roi) or a measurement to a hand-drawn area.
Turns each detected point into a disc (or a distance-bounded region) and labels it — a segmentation seeded by a detector.
radius in µm, or per point from a column such as a fitted sigma.
A Laplacian-of-Gaussian blob detector between min and max radius (µm); threshold is on the normalized response.
Each detection is a Point row (y, x, sigma, intensity). Points, not pixels — nothing is segmented.
Local maxima at least min_distance apart above a threshold, with optional sub-pixel refinement.
Fast and simple — the choice when particles are well separated.

Cuts the Z-stack into overlapping slabs, flattens each (max/mean/min), finds bright spots in 2-D per slab, then fits every hit on the raw stack: a split Gaussian in z (a confocal axial profile is skewed) and a 2-D Gaussian in x,y for the sub-voxel centroid and the apparent size.

Keeps only what is bead-shaped for the given diameter: hot voxels, aggregates, fibres, the scan line and the haze planted in this phantom are all refused, as are the beads whose brightest plane lies outside the stack.
Auto slabs get thinner as the field gets denser; drag Bead diameter away from 1 µm and watch the size filter refuse the real beads.
The Euclidean distance transform of a mask: every foreground pixel's distance to the nearest background pixel, in µm.
Shown as a heat map over the image; the watershed uses it to split touching objects.
A band of given width along each label's boundary — for measuring the periphery, or a ring around the nucleus.
Every label's outline as ordered boundary points — a contour you can measure, plot or rasterize.
Partitions the plane among the detected points: every pixel joins its nearest point's cell, up to max_distance.
bound limits the cells to a mask, to each region, or (here) to the whole frame.
Builds a mesh: one closed surface per label by marching cubes (label_surface), or a hull / alpha shape / Voronoi cell around each cluster of points.
A surface is volumetric, so the input must be a Z-stack; shown here on 3-D-labelled nuclei.
The mesh overlay draws the vertices that lie near the viewed plane.
One point per label at its centroid, carrying the label's measurements — the bridge from regions to a point cloud.
Interpolates a point field's columns (u, v, strain…) onto the pixel grid as Voxel layers.
Shown: the PIV displacement of a warped speckle pair, rasterized and colour-mapped.

transform.rasterize_mesh.slow_reason: meshing a 3-D label volume then voxelising it takes seconds
features: Fills each mesh element back into a label raster — the inverse of Tessellate's label surface.
Moves an attribute between domains: a per-label value onto its voxels, a per-frame value onto its labels, and so on.
Moves an attribute across the structure spine — Voxel ↔ Label ↔ Point ↔ Track, or any of them onto Frame — reducing when it coarsens.
Shown: each nucleus' measured area carried onto the track it belongs to (mean over the track's members).
Per-label statistics (area, centroid, intensity mean / min / max / std, shape descriptors) as a Label table.
The raw input lets you measure intensities on the unprocessed image while using processed labels.
target = point measures around detected points instead.
Per-object derived metrics: velocity and speed (µm/s) from the object's track, K-nearest-neighbour distances (µm), local divergence / curl, and intensity fold changes.
Speed needs a correspondence between frames, so a tracker runs upstream; the frame interval comes from the file.
Interpolates per-object quantities (density, speed, divergence, mean area, intensity) onto a regular grid of points — a continuous field from discrete objects.
Motion fields need tracks upstream; density and intensity do not.
Reduces one column of a table to a single number per series (mean, sum, count, …) — the scalar a sweep optimises.
Groups points into n_clusters by k-means; each point gets a cluster id to colour by.

analysis.accumulate_field.slow_reason: a DVC increment series takes many seconds
features: Sums frame-to-frame displacement increments into a cumulative field.
Keeps or drops whole labels by one measured column: a fixed cut, a percentile, or a cut derived from the population.
Ids are preserved (label 5 stays label 5), so tables measured upstream still join.
Routes each label (or point) to a pass or a fail layer by up to four column conditions.
Shown: nuclei with area > 250 px² pass; move the slider to see the split.
Groups a table's rows (by frame, by position, by a column) and reduces a value column with one or more reducers.
Stacks several tables with matching columns into one — frames of a series, or the same measurement on several files.
Joins the other dataset's table onto this one by id (and frame), prefixing its columns.
Shown: the measured nuclei joined with the plain label table of the same field.
Links labels (or points) frame to frame into tracks: nearest centroid, overlap, topology, fingerprint or SerialTrack.
max_distance bounds a step; max_frame_gap lets a track survive a missed frame.
Shown at frame 3: each nucleus' path so far.
A simple linker: nearest neighbour within max_distance, or best IoU overlap.
Per-track velocity and, from neighbouring tracks, a local strain — the deformation of a moving sheet of cells.
Particle image velocimetry: cross-correlates windows of each frame with the previous (or a fixed) frame to get a displacement per window.
Shown at t = 1: arrows for the sinusoidal warp between the two speckle frames.

analysis.dic_correlate.slow_reason: the ALDIC solver takes seconds per frame
features: Digital image correlation (pyALDIC): a dense displacement and strain field between a reference and each frame.
Digital volume correlation (ALDVC): the 3-D counterpart of DIC, on subsets of a volume.
Dense optical flow (TV-L1) between consecutive frames: a displacement per pixel, written as Voxel layers.
Shown: the flow magnitude at t = 1.
A scatter / line plot of two table columns, grouped by a third; the figure is a raster Dataset you can view or write.
A histogram / distribution of one column, optionally per group.
One column over time, one line per object or per group.
A grid of one value column indexed by two others — objects × frames, for instance.
Richardson–Lucy deconvolution with a PSF built from the objective NA, the emission wavelength and the Z step — all read from the file.
More iterations sharpen further but amplify noise.

enhance.zs_deconvnet.slow_reason: trains a zero-shot network on the image first
features: Zero-shot deconvolution: trains a small network on this image alone, then applies it; no clean reference needed.
Estimates the background surface (rolling ball, opening, Gaussian, polynomial, percentile…) and subtracts or divides it out.
The regions input (a drawn region) can instead sample what counts as background and zero it.
Equalises the brightness of every frame of a series against a sliding window — bleaching and lamp flicker removed.
Rescales intensities to a window: by percentiles of the histogram, or by absolute low / high values.
A power-law transfer: gamma < 1 lifts the dim, > 1 compresses it. Display-like, but it changes the data.
Contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalisation on a grid of tiles; clip_limit caps the local amplification.
A Gaussian blur with σ in microns — the same µm give the same smoothing on any objective.
Around 0.5 µm denoises lightly; 2 µm flattens the nuclei.
White top-hat: the image minus its opening, keeping only features smaller than the radius — the uneven background falls away.
Difference of Gaussians: a band-pass that keeps structures between the two σ — spots of one size class.
Detects bright blobs in a radius band and paints them out with the surrounding intensity — removes puncta or debris before segmenting.
Divides by a heavily blurred copy of the series to remove illumination falloff; bg_floor avoids amplifying the dark corners.
A median filter: removes salt-and-pepper noise while keeping edges.
Edge-preserving smoothing: averages neighbours that are close in space AND in intensity.
Non-local means: averages patches that look alike wherever they are; h sets how different two patches may be.
Total-variation denoising: smooths noise while keeping sharp edges; weight trades noise against detail.
Shrinks wavelet coefficients to remove noise at every scale; the mode picks the shrinkage rule.
Unsharp masking: adds amount × (image − blur) to sharpen edges.
Grey-level erosion, dilation, opening or closing with a disc of the given radius.
Dilation minus erosion: an edge map whose thickness is the radius.
Crops to a mask, drawn regions or a label raster instead of a rectangle: keep the frame and blank outside (frame), shrink to the box around the regions (fit), or one window per object (each).
Shown: the field blanked outside the segmented nuclei.
Pixel arithmetic between this image and another branch's image (or a constant when Other is unwired): add, subtract, multiply, divide, min, max, difference, mean.
Shown: the field minus a copy of itself shifted by (4, 3) px — the edges light up.
Set algebra on masks: subtract, union, intersect, xor or invert, between two Voxel layers on this wire or one from a second branch.
Shown: the Otsu mask minus the local-threshold mask of the same field.
Arithmetic on the numbers a Dataset carries — a scalar, a table column, a per-plane layer — against another one or a constant, with units carried through.
Shown: max_intensity ÷ mean_intensity per nucleus, as a new column peak_ratio.
